whatItFakes: Officials' automatic hires (an aide at the monthly staff review, a department head refilled at the executive's review) choose only among people out of work, though anyone paid less than the post would apply.
why: Taking a public post ends the person's current job, and the core doesn't yet release the records that rely on a job (a business's visitor contracts name its workers' jobs), so ending one mid-contract breaks the finance check.
replacement: Resolved Oct 19: taking a public post ends the job the person held (startPublicJob), so an aide, a department head and a state cabinet nominee may come from a private job when the post pays more than they earn; someone who has worked today leaves for a post tomorrow. Shown in staff-hire-employed.test.ts (pool item gov-stopgap-staff-missing-engine).

whatItFakes: On a minimum wage's effective date the laws module replaces each underpaid work commitment's hourly rate directly in core work state.
why: core2 has no pay-change path: admitWorkCommitment is the only writer and no API ends or re-rates a commitment.
replacement: OPUS-CORE's work pay-change API (re-rate a commitment from a date with its source), called here instead. Resolved 2026-10-13: Replaced by OPUS-CORE's rerateJob (core2-api-v12) in laws.ts raiseOne and raiseToFloor; counted residents' jobs rise too.

whatItFakes: A state or federal officeholder outside the town is a stable identity (name, gender, birth date, party) with no core2 person behind it.
why: core2 has no fill-in yet: a named person outside the town can't become a full person when clicked. Resolved by OPUS-OFFICIALS (2026-10-13): every state and federal official outside the town is filled in at the opening as a full person with traits, views, a party wing, a career and colleagues (src/core2/modules/officials.ts); a holder seated later is filled in the first time their seat is read.
replacement: CORE's two-level fill-in builds the full person from this identity (seeded from the world and the seat), with kin and a past from PEOPLE.

whatItFakes: A law whose first recorded phase begins after the January 20, 2025 start (most income tax, sales tax, property tax, SNAP, unemployment and Medicaid rows begin October 2025 or January 2026) is in force from the start at that phase's terms, labeled as an estimate.
why: The starting-law research was compiled for a 2026 start; the owner moved the start to January 20, 2025 on October 14, 2026, and a law in force must never be unknown.
replacement: Oct 23, 2026 (research-law-reach-sourced-parameters): the phases in force on January 20, 2025 are now sourced and built for the federal income tax and Social Security wage base (IRS Rev. Proc. 2024-40, Publication 15 2025), every state's income and sales tax and average local sales tax (Tax Foundation, January 1, 2025), SNAP maximums (USDA FNS FY2025), the Medicaid match for all 56 places (HHS FY2025, FR Doc. 2023-25636 and 2024-27938) and unemployment weekly bounds (DOL, January 2025), in data/research/laws/*-2025-*.json, written by scripts/research/build-starting-law.py and checked by scripts/research/check-start-law-2025.ts; rowsCarriedToStart in src/core2/modules/laws.ts no longer reaches those series. Still carried back (research-start-law-remaining-2025-phases): county and city income taxes, city sales taxes, county, city and some state minimum-wage tiers, state corporate income tax, local income tax authority, unemployment program terms, and the five territories' income and sales taxes.

whatItFakes: The end of each term in progress at the opening for state and local offices: the seats of a body take turns over the years in one term that the office's calendar (the county schedule or the state's municipal election law) holds elections, and each term ends on the start day after its seat's election; where a state's own start rule isn't read, January 1 (the governors' clauses of AK, CA, CO, DE, FL, HI, IL, IN, LA, MD, ME, NJ, OH, OK, PA, VA, WA and WI, and, as estimates from the usual clause and the current governor's date, AZ, CT, GA, ID, KS, MN, MT, NE, NV, OR, TX, UT, VT and WY are read, in data/elections/term-starts.json). Federal terms are read: every House seat ends January 3 of an odd year (amend. XX), Senate seats by their real class, the presidency on January 20.
why: Real election calendars and term-start dates for each office are M2's filing and election work.
replacement: Oct 23, 2026 (research-offices-sourced-parameters): every place's governor clause (the mayor's for D.C.) and the day its legislators take their seats are now read into src/core2/data/elections/term-starts.json, with the URL and quoted text of each (48 governor rows and 43 legislature rows SOURCED; 8 and 13 ESTIMATED where the text sets no day and an inauguration or session date stands in, or, for Florida, Hawaii and Tennessee, where the text starts the term on election day itself and ruleStartAfter, which takes the first start after election day, uses the day after: one day late). Still open: municipal offices, whose start day is each charter's or the state's municipal law's, and county offices where county-election-schedule-by-state.json has no row, still start on the table's default of January 1. Earlier text: The other states' governor start clauses and the state-legislature start days read into data/elections/term-starts.json, and municipal timing from the 92O baselines (county bodies are read: county-election-schedule-by-state.json).

whatItFakes: A special election for a seat no race engine counts (a statewide executive seat, a judge, a seat of another body) goes to the best-suited eligible person on the day instead of a vote. The town's own seats are real races in the voting engine, and a House or legislative district outside the town is counted by the world races (named party candidates, the winner serves the unexpired term). The date is the state's law for the office where special-election-law.json reads it, else the 90-day estimate (SG-GOV-special-election-timing).
why: The world races count only House and legislative districts; the other kinds have no counted race yet. Narrowed Oct 19 (claude/special-election-races).
replacement: Each office's special-election timing from its law (many fill at the next general election).

whatItFakes: Every adult resident counts as a registered voter where filing or signing requires registration.
why: core2 has no voter registration record yet. Retired by Session C, October 15, 2026: the eligibility check inferred registration solely from age and residence. The owner's no-paperwork rule does not call for a registration mechanic. Filing no longer reports that invented status; sourced research metadata is retained.
replacement: Retired the unsupported registered-voter eligibility result. Age, residence, deadlines, party membership and term limits remain separate checks. Reintroduce a registration mechanic only if the owner or golden path calls for it, with actual records.

whatItFakes: A person's opening stance on a policy question is their lean times the question's measured left-right axis, plus, for the eight questions the CES 2020 has an item for, a stored opening record with its reasons (src/core2/modules/views.ts openingRecord, data/research/people/opening-stance-loadings.json) holding what their faith and four-year degree add beyond the lean. Every other question, and every person with no recorded faith or schooling, opens as the lean alone, and no trait loading exists because the CES has no personality measure.
why: OPUS-PEOPLE's views engine (values and stances formed from each person's life) isn't on core2 yet.
replacement: Per-question opening records for the questions the survey did not ask (a source with loadings for each), until every question opens as a stored record formed from the person's life.

whatItFakes: An ad reaches the adults with the fewest work hours, as a stand-in for who watches and scrolls most; ad time is bought from a stand-in local media seller.
why: People's media habits and the news outlets aren't modeled on core2 yet. Resolved Oct 16: ad time is bought from the press's town outlet and reaches that outlet's followers; with no press there is no outlet, so nothing is bought. The stand-in seller and the fewest-work-hours viewers are deleted.
replacement: Each person's media habits and real outlets (PEOPLE and the news engine); ads bought from those outlets.

whatItFakes: Where the town records no professional-services business (NAICS 5419 includes public opinion polling), a campaign's poll interviews are paid to a stand-in pollster organization in town.
why: Small towns often have no polling firm; the region's businesses outside the town aren't recorded as sellers a campaign can reach.
replacement: The region's or state's real polling firms as recorded organizations a campaign buys from. Researched Oct 23, 2026 (research-elections-sourced-parameters): data/research/elections/cbp-2023-campaign-sellers.json holds the U.S. Census Bureau's County Business Patterns 2023 establishment counts for NAICS 541910 (polling) and 541820 (public relations) for all 56 places and by county: 4,419 polling establishments nationally, published in only 260 of 3,246 county equivalents, so a town's own pollster is the exception. The builder item elections-campaign-sellers-beyond-town reads it in src/core2/modules/campaigns.ts seller() (town, then county, then state) in place of the stand-in.

whatItFakes: Where the town records no professional-services or manufacturing business (direct mail advertising, NAICS 54186; printing, NAICS 323), a campaign's mailers are paid to a stand-in mail house in town, postage included.
why: The region's printers and mail houses outside the town aren't recorded as sellers, and postage isn't paid to a postal organization.
replacement: The region's printers and mail houses as recorded sellers, with postage paid to the Postal Service's account. Researched Oct 23, 2026 (research-elections-sourced-parameters): data/research/elections/cbp-2023-campaign-sellers.json holds County Business Patterns 2023 counts for NAICS 541860 (direct mail, 1,705 establishments in 166 county equivalents) and 323111 (commercial printing, 15,271 in 837) for all 56 places and by county. The builder item elections-campaign-sellers-beyond-town reads it in src/core2/modules/campaigns.ts seller() and sendMail(), and pays the postage share to a Postal Service organization.

whatItFakes: Where the town records no recreation, lodging or food-service business, a campaign event's venue rent is paid to a stand-in venue in town.
why: Public halls (a town's own community center, a school gym) aren't recorded as places a campaign rents.
replacement: The town's public buildings and halls as rentable places with their fee schedules, and the region's venues. Researched Oct 23, 2026 (research-elections-sourced-parameters): data/research/elections/cbp-2023-campaign-sellers.json holds County Business Patterns 2023 counts for NAICS 713, 721, 722, 722320 and 813410 for all 56 places: food services and drinking places are published in 3,152 of 3,246 county equivalents, so a stand-in is needed only where the town records none. No public hall fee schedule was sourced; the builder item elections-campaign-sellers-beyond-town reads the counts in src/core2/modules/campaigns.ts seller() and records the town's own halls.

whatItFakes: A world candidate's campaign day (rivalDay) never holds a donor meeting at a supporter's home; its money comes only from call time, the turn's asks and the outside donors. Because rivalDay never takes it, campaignDayChoices with world=true skips the host scoring entirely (src/core2/campaign-day.ts, same marker) and reports the donor-meeting choice unavailable with no host, so a rival's turn reads nobody's circle for it.
why: The donor meeting was built for the player's campaign first (campaign-like-real-races, phase A: named donors at house parties); scoring it in the rival's day changes every world race's money and pace, which wants its own calibration run.
replacement: campaignDayChoices names a host for world candidates too (the world=true skip in campaign-day.ts is deleted), rivalDay scores the donor-meeting choice on the same scale as the event and the interview (rising as the bank empties and with the host's warmth), takes it as the day's whole act when it scores best, and the world's races are re-checked against the campaign-finance calibration.

whatItFakes: In a nonpartisan or local race, voters the world doesn't name vote as lean bands around the place's lean, sized from the town's population times the 2024 share of people who voted, each band voting with its named people. (Partisan state and federal races now count them in blocks: src/core2/electorate-blocks.ts.) The figures are researched: 0.46 of residents vote on a presidential date, scaled by cycle (midterm 0.72, off-cycle 0.39; Hajnal and Green 2024); what stays a stand-in is the local groups themselves.
why: CORE's voter groups exist as a table but generated worlds don't populate them yet. Resolved by the one-electorate change (owner, Oct 14, 2026): the lean bands and the group store are deleted; the rest of a local race's electorate (the town's population past its counted residents) votes on the counted residents' own engine (src/core2/electorate.ts countPlaces), and no race sizes its electorate from a share of population any more.
replacement: CORE's populated voter groups (counts by place, age, job and household, with lean and turnout), each voting as a group.

whatItFakes: When filing closes, a statewide partisan race with no candidate of one major party gets that party's nominee: a named official, or a person filled in to run for it.
why: Candidacy decides who runs from people's own records, in every world since engine map line 23; how a party recruits a statewide nominee where no member of that side filed is not built.
replacement: PEOPLE's who-runs decisions file each candidate through fileCandidacy with recorded reasons; incumbents decide the same way.

whatItFakes: Counties and cities start their fiscal year on their state's date.
why: City and county fiscal calendars aren't researched yet (M1-budgets-taxes research item 1).
replacement: Each county's and city's own fiscal year start and adoption deadline, from charters and budget documents, with estimates for the rest. Resolved by OPUS-GOV, Oct 12: each county and city takes its state's same-type Census 2024 sampled unit nearest in population (src/core2/data/budgets/local-fiscal-years.json), else the national most common year end.

whatItFakes: Local spending is shared between county and city by function (counties: welfare, health and hospitals, corrections, highways, natural resources; cities and townships: the rest), and local revenue in the same proportion.
why: Census reports local government finances combined, not by government. Resolved by OPUS-GOV (2026-10-13): each function divides between county and city by the state's shares in the Census 2022 Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances by type of government (data/research/budgets/local-spending-by-type.json).
replacement: Census FY2024 individual government finances (data/source/government-finances) for each county and city, with estimates for the rest.

whatItFakes: Each new fiscal year's budget is adopted on its start date by carrying the year's amounts forward.
why: Councils and legislatures can't vote budgets until M3 (owner, Oct 10: old budget rules until councils vote).
replacement: The council's or legislature's budget vote (M3-05) and the executive's priorities.

whatItFakes: A mayor's veto is overridden by two thirds of the members voting; ordinances take effect 30 days after enactment.
why: Each city's charter sets its own override majority and effective date; they aren't read yet.
replacement: Override majorities and ordinance effective dates from each state's municipal code and sampled charters, with estimates for the rest. Resolved by OPUS-GOV, Oct 12: two thirds of each body's whole membership (vetoOverrideShare, sourced in FIXER's stand-in figures).

whatItFakes: Committee seats go to each party's most senior members by the chamber's party ratio; real committees are appointed by the presiding officer or a committee on committees. Committee size is now sourced (about 11 members, 5 to 20; Book of the States 2023, Table 3.23).
why: Each body's committee rules, sizes, assignments and chairs aren't read yet.
replacement: Leadership already seats committees in play (src/core2/modules/leadership.ts assigner(), from each chamber template's assignmentAuthority in data/research/legislature/chamber-leadership.json); seniority seating is the fallback in committeeStage when no leadership roster exists. Research done Oct 23, 2026: each chamber's own appointing rule is in data/research/gov/chamber-committee-appointment-2026.json (108 chambers; 27 SOURCED from the chamber's adopted rules or its legislature's official page, 16 of which seat committees through another hand than the template: a committee on committees, the majority leader, seniority, a chamber vote, the party caucuses or each committee's chair; the rest ESTIMATED as the template default), checked by scripts/research/legislature-local-rules-check.ts. assigner() reading the chamber's row is the builder item gov-leadership-committee-appointer-by-chamber. Stays open until it does and the remaining chambers are read.

whatItFakes: On a statewide ballot measure, the voters the world doesn't name vote as even lean bands around the state's 2024 presidential lean, sized by the state's 2024 vote, each band voting its own view of the question (no separate public-opinion level for the policy).
why: CORE's voter groups aren't populated in generated worlds, and OPUS-PEOPLE's views engine (with issue opinion beyond left-right) isn't built.
replacement: CORE's populated voter groups across the state, each voting from PEOPLE's views of the question.

whatItFakes: A recall petition's required signatures read the state's named base from the world's records where it holds them (votes cast for the office, or at the town's last election of that level, from the recorded results). Where it holds none, the base is sized from the real averages: registered voters (the town's eligible voters times the national registration share), the last gubernatorial vote (the town's population times the voting share, scaled to a midterm), and votes cast before the town has held an election.
why: The world keeps no voter rolls and does not keep a statewide race's votes by town, and a new town has held no election yet. The counted residents sign and vote by the same rule as named people, and the base is a whole count of voters.
replacement: Registered voters read from the town's rolls and the town's share of the last gubernatorial vote read from the state's returns, once the world keeps them.

whatItFakes: An employers' group's lobbyist is the owner of the member business the bill costs most (when they live in town, are not barred and their traits lean to serve), else the best-paid town resident working for it; the group does not hire one.
why: Owners now decide to join and pay dues (Oct 14), but lobbyists aren't a hired job yet.
replacement: The group hires a lobbyist (a person with a job, a record and memory of each member's votes). Owner as lobbyist done Oct 19.

whatItFakes: What an organization stands for when it weighs a candidate for endorsement is read from the little its engine keeps: a cause group's topic, for it unless its founder's drive wants a repeal (a desired change like building a park or cutting a hazard counts as for); an employers' group formed over a wage bill states nothing, so it endorses no one; a party chapter holds its lean along the 54 platform questions only, so a budget-line plank weighs nothing with it. Only a group's full members hear its endorsement and are asked to volunteer; counted residents who hold the same cause are not reached.
why: No group engine yet writes a group platform (a candidate questionnaire, a slate of positions) or keeps the question an employers' wage group argued, and groups enlist only full people.
replacement: Each organization keeps its own platform (the positions its members adopt, a questionnaire it sends candidates) that the endorsement weighing reads, and its counted supporters are reached by the same rule times their count.

whatItFakes: A staffer hired where no government treasury is open (no budgets module) holds the post without pay; with budgets open they're on the payroll of the government their official serves.
why: Public payroll from government treasuries isn't wired in core2 yet (requested from OPUS-CORE).
replacement: Resolved Oct 20: a staffer whose office employer sits where no job exists to follow (a territory's state or federal office) takes the town's schedule and payday (scheduleFromPlaceId), so every aide hired where budgets are open is on a treasury payroll. Shown in staff-paid-every-place.test.ts (pool item gov-stopgap-staff-missing-engine).

whatItFakes: A race the town doesn't vote in is counted on the counted residents' engine at a coarser level (a House district's, the state's counties', a legislative district's eligible voters, voting as the town's counted residents would on each place's 2024 lean), but its candidates are each party's typical candidate (the holder stands for their party with the typical campaign) rather than people with records, and a state legislative district with no read result is the state's vote over its districts leaning to its holder's party at the typical margin.
why: Fictional candidates with records for every seat in the country aren't built (PEOPLE's who runs), and state legislative district results aren't read.
replacement: Each race's candidates as fictional people with records and campaigns, and each legislative district's own 2024 result.

whatItFakes: A territory's governor race outside the town's own is not run, so its governor serves on past the election its law holds (Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and the U.S. Virgin Islands elect one in November 2026).
why: The territories have no counted electorate places (no presidential vote or county places on record) and no major-party record for their governors; their own parties (Puerto Rico's New Progressive and Popular Democratic, for one) are not modeled.
replacement: Superseded Oct 30, 2026 by SG-GOV-territory-legislature-race (gov-every-state-and-town-governs U1): governorRaces is deleted and another place's governor is raced through racesIn's one seat loop in src/core2/modules/voting.ts, whose territory check skips a territory's governor with its legislative and statewide executive seats under that row; the replacement (each territory's electorate places from its own governor, legislative or delegate results, and its own parties, on the same counted engine) is that row's.

whatItFakes: Another state's governor race is run on the counted engine and its winner's party is kept on the seat from the state's inauguration day, but no engine acts as that state's executive: no budget, signature or appointment there reads the new governor, and the officials roster keeps the governor seated at the opening.
why: Other states' governments are not yet played at a coarser level; only Congress outside the town is read back (src/core2/modules/legislature.ts reads the world races' seats).
replacement: Resolved Oct 30, 2026 (gov-every-state-and-town-governs U1, the laws lead's decision B): every other state's governor is held on the offices engine's term from the opening (seatOutsideOffices in src/core2/modules/offices.ts), and racesIn's one seat loop in src/core2/modules/voting.ts races the governor's seat by the same rule as every other statewide office (governorRaces is deleted), so seatRaceWinner seats the winner on that term through seatWinner, the one term writer, at home in that state; the voting engine's own seats table is no longer written for a governor, and the race reads the incumbent's party from the serving term. The officials roster's separate governor is gone. A coarse executive acting for each other state (budget, signature, appointment) is the world-governing plan's U3 (SG-GOV-other-legislatures-not-sitting).

whatItFakes: A presidential year's national environment is a fixed shift against the party holding the presidency, with no economy or presidential record behind it.
why: WORLD's economy and the president's record don't feed the race yet; the shift is the campaign parameter presidentialIncumbentPartyShift (TUNABLE). Resolved by SIM-ELECTORATE (2026-10-13): every state's presidential vote is counted in its counties' blocks, and the national environment is read from the economy since the opening (WORLD macro) and the candidates' records (src/core2/electorate-blocks.ts); the missing approval is SG-GOV-electorate-approval.
replacement: A national environment read from the economy (WORLD macro) and the president's record, replacing the fixed incumbent-party shift.

whatItFakes: Paid family leave collects the same estimated payroll premium from full workers and counted groups but pays no leave. The generic contribution omits jurisdiction-specific employee/employer splits, wage caps and covered-employment exclusions. Nobody claims leave for a birth, adoption or a relative's illness; no received contribution notice or director explanation is modeled.
why: There is no birth-leave or caregiving event a worker can claim leave from, and no benefit payment route from a treasury to a person.
replacement: PEOPLE: a leave-taking choice on a birth or a relative's serious illness (health engine), and CORE: a benefit payment from a government treasury to a person through the journal (e.g. payBenefit(treasuryId, personId, amountMinor, source)); then GOV pays wage replacement from the premium fund.

whatItFakes: Public-sector collective bargaining raises public workers' pay by an estimated union premium phased in over the first contract years (src/core2/law-reach/group-a-bargaining.ts), but no contract is bargained: there is no bargaining table, unit or negotiation, and the premium is one average for every public job.
why: There is no bargaining engine: no union contract, no bargaining unit wage or table.
replacement: GOV: a bargaining engine that negotiates the unit's contract with the public employer and applies it with CORE's rerateJob(jobId, hourlyMinor, source) (builder item gov-public-sector-bargaining); WORLD: union membership on workers' records (world-union-membership-record). Oct 23, 2026: the band the counted public workers' union share checks against is sourced in data/research/laws/bls-2025-union-public-sector.json (BLS Union Members 2025: public sector 32.9 percent in 2025, 32.2 in 2024; private 5.9; union median weekly earnings $1,404 against $1,174 nonunion), checked by scripts/research/check-law-reach-sources.ts.
resolution: A recognized public unit's contract is bargained at its funding government's budget date: the unit's pay rises by the growth of the employer's own budget line through rerateJob, only where the law is in force, and a repeal stops the next contract (src/core2/law-reach/group-a-bargaining.ts). Strikes and member stances are not built.

whatItFakes: A right-to-work law lowers the local union's dues as membership falls (about four points over five years), but no worker's membership or fee is recorded: the dues are one pooled flow from the wider population, and a named worker keeps paying or not paying exactly as before.
why: Union membership and dues are not on workers' records; the local's dues are one standing flow set from the state's membership rate (src/core2/membership-dues.ts). The law's effect is read by the group A union mechanic (src/core2/law-reach/group-a-union.ts), which scales that flow.
replacement: WORLD or CORE: union membership on named jobs and counted groups, dues as a payroll deduction through the journal, which right-to-work then ends for nonmembers (builder item world-union-membership-record). Oct 23, 2026: the membership rate it reads by state is already sourced on main (BLS Union Members 2025, Table 5: data/research/business/bls-union-2025.json, read through src/core2/data/business/union-membership.json by src/core2/membership-dues.ts); no new figure was needed.

whatItFakes: Legal cannabis sales move each household's spending (about $170 per resident a year, estimated from 2024 state sales) from outside the town to the town's existing retail businesses, split by their demand. There are no dedicated licensed dispensaries and no license application. A named adult's use is a seeded draw from their id at the national adult prevalence (src/core2/modules/place-prices.ts), not a state series or a stored record.
why: The place-prices engine reads the law monthly (src/core2/modules/place-prices.ts). The use draw is national, not by state; dispensaries are not founded as businesses.
replacement: WORLD: dispensaries founded through the business engine and licensed by the control board (laws-cannabis-dispensaries); PEOPLE: each place's own adult share in place of the national one, read by usesCannabis and cannabisWeight in src/core2/modules/place-prices.ts (builder item prices-cannabis-state-prevalence). Oct 23, 2026: the per-place table is sourced for all 56 places in data/research/laws/samhsa-2024-cannabis-past-year.json (SAMHSA NSDUH 2023-2024, Table 2, past-year use, 18+; territories at the median of the 51 surveyed places, marked estimate), and the national pricesCannabisUsePrevalence is 0.2317 (Total U.S. 18+), checked by scripts/research/check-law-reach-sources.ts.

whatItFakes: The credit engine reads the catalog cap when quoting new personal loans for full and counted households, under the state's question where the town's chain governs and Congress's consumer-loan interest question everywhere. The generic 36% ceiling stands in for product, principal, fee and lender-specific statutory rules. Counted income uses contracted wages adjusted by the latest settled wage-flow fraction; individual counted attendance and historical earnings ledgers are absent. Existing fixed-rate contracts are not retroactively repriced.
why: Personal loans share the borrowing comparison and use borrower-keyed payments in both tiers. Lender exemptions, fee-inclusive APR, statutory product scope and counted individual attendance history are missing. A binding native rate change, received explanation and director chain still need evidence. Measured: the generic ceiling (36 percent, `consumerLoanRateCap`) sits far above the quoted personal-loan rate (policy rate plus 3.08 and 6 points, about 13 percent at today's rates), so `min(marketRate, ceiling)` never binds in an ordinary rate year and a borrower is never offered a changed rate; a received explanation can only fire once product-specific caps (payday and installment loans, fees included) or a rate shock make the ceiling bind.
replacement: Counted earnings history matching full workers, sourced product-specific rate and fee rules, and a named borrower receiving the explanation and discussing the changed offer.

whatItFakes: The construction engine reads multifamily zoning at each monthly starts decision; a completed home reaching a named household and its informed reaction still need played-world proof.
why: A changed starts calculation is not itself a household housed; the full law-to-person chain remains unproven.
replacement: WORLD: a housing engine with lots, units and construction decisions (e.g. addHousingCapacity(placeId, units) driven by builders' returns).

whatItFakes: Housing spending pays rent help to the lowest-cash renting households the extra money covers (a monthly payment from the treasury to the household's head, no more than the rent), but only to full households: counted renting households are not reached.
why: Counted renters have no per-household lease to pay toward; they are pooled flows.
replacement: Counted renting households read by the same rule, times their count, once counted rent flows are keyed per household (world-counted-law-payouts-keyed).
resolution: housing-assistance.ts pays rent help from the housing line to the lowest-cash renting households, full ones directly and counted ones times the households they stand for through countedPayment, and records each with lawApplied.

whatItFakes: The inclusionary law now sets construction shares and returns, but the completed-unit allocation handles full leases only.
why: Counted households must use the same affordable-unit allocation, and a paid rent change needs a received notice and director line.
replacement: WORLD: the housing engine's new units, with the set-aside share priced below market for eligible households.

whatItFakes: Rent renewal reads stabilization for full leases and counted rent flows, but applies the catalog's estimated cap to every rented building. A full tenant gets a renewal notice (the law, old rent, market rent, charged rent) and learns of the saving; a counted tenant gets no notice.
why: Building exemptions and enacted cap terms are not yet resolved; a counted tenant is not a person who can be told.

replacement: Resolved Oct 23, 2026 (research-offices-sourced-parameters): the 60 rows were each checked against a fetched page (each office's Ballotpedia page, or the state's or territory's official site, with Wikipedia once for the U.S. Virgin Islands Board of Education roster), and each row in data/research/offices/statewide-executive-parties-2026.json now carries its page, a quote and the holder on January 20, 2025 and January 1, 2026. 54 matched; 6 were corrected (Arizona's lieutenant governor and the Northern Marianas' are partisan-ballot offices, Guam's attorney general is nonpartisan, the Virgin Islands boards of education and elections print party labels, and the Georgia labor commissioner's seat was vacant on the opening day). Read by statewidePartyOf in src/core2/offices-state.ts, which seats each office's party at the opening. Original replacement: Every row checked against Ballotpedia's partisan composition pages or the state's own records.

whatItFakes: Each month, a state, county, city or federal treasury receives from the town's outside account an even twelfth of the yearly revenue no flow in the game pays (state and federal aid come from the treasury above it; corporate, customs, excise, estate and gift, selective sales and vehicle taxes, and charges and fees, come from named groups of payers on their due dates), and pays each spending line an even twelfth: what the town's engines paid on the line stays in town, the town's share of purchases goes to its businesses, and the rest goes to the outside account as spending elsewhere.
why: Real payers outside the town (the rest of the state's taxpayers) and real payees (contractors and public workers elsewhere) aren't modeled; their real dates (aid schedules, tax due dates, payrolls) aren't in data yet.
replacement: Each revenue line from its real payer on its real dates, and each spending line to its real payees on theirs.

whatItFakes: A government's charges and fees (tuition, hospital bills, sewer and trash, parks, tolls) are paid by the town's households in proportion to the living cost each pays on the 1st, split by what the charges are for from the Census 2022 item codes; no household chooses to use a service, no business pays a charge of its own, and a household that uses none still pays its share of the living cost.
why: gov-outside-revenue-fees-wiring (p1): the fees line was an even twelfth from the outside account that no household or business paid. The game does not yet model each service's use (a student's tuition, a hospital stay, a sewer bill by dwelling), so the charges follow what a household spends.
replacement: Each service paid by the people who use it on the day they use it: tuition by enrolled students' households, hospital charges by patients' visits, sewer and trash by dwellings and businesses, parks and tolls by trips, from the school, health and travel engines. (pool item gov-service-charges-by-use).

whatItFakes: The national mood that moves every voter's choice for the president's party is read from the national economy since the opening (unemployment and inflation) and the midterm penalty, with no presidential approval behind it.
why: No engine records the president's approval yet (the executive's record and the public's view of it).
replacement: Presidential approval read from the president's own record and the public's views (the executive engine and the views engine), moving the president's party's candidates by its measured effect on the vote.

whatItFakes: A township board's ordinances are written as the town's own local law (the place level of the law chain), and a township board only legislates where no town council does; the law chain has no township level, so a township's ordinances and a village council's inside it can't both stand.
why: Towns governed by a township board never legislated at all: only councils and county boards met (Oct 13 lawmaking-volume fix).
replacement: A township level in the law chain (laws-starting.ts) with its own starting law and enactments, so a township board and a village council inside it each legislate for their own jurisdiction.

whatItFakes: The opening's public employers in town (schools, police, fire, county offices) pay their workers from outside accounts; the treasury's lines for that work pay the outside account instead of those employers.
why: Linking the opening's public employers to a treasury is a core change (public owner records, work-cash.ts; SG-P8-public-payroll-due-flow).
replacement: Each public employer draws its payroll from its government's treasury, and the close counts it as that line's in-town spending. Resolved by Claude Sonnet session, October 16, 2026: the budgets engine calls api.fundPublicPay for every opening public employer, linking it to its government's treasury (matched by government key); the employer's wages leave the treasury's account on the payday journal, the close counts them as that line's in-town spending, and what the treasury couldn't cover is a public-pay shortfall on the month's treasury row. What the lines still pay the outside account is spending outside the town's employers.

whatItFakes: When the federal Social Security line is cut or raised, the retirement awards the opening wrote for full people keep their amount; only awards claimed during play follow the line.
why: The finance engine refuses to change the amount of a recipient-income contract (setStandingContractAmount in finance-state.ts, OPUS-CORE). Resolved Oct 16, 2026 (core-opening-award-level-rerate): a recipient income contract takes a new amount from its next due date (setRecipientIncomeAmount), the measure and day are recorded beside the saved award, and the outside funding that pays its payer moves by the same dollars; applySocialSecurityLevel sets them.
replacement: setStandingContractAmount accepts a recipient-income contract's new benefit level from its next due date, and applySocialSecurityLevel sets it, with the funding contract that pays it.

whatItFakes: The public pay floor's employer-to-level map is a first cut (public schools count as town employers). A public post filled by the government (an aide, a department head) is paid at the floor in force the day it is filled, and a jobs-engine opening at the floor in force the day it is posted. Councils, legislatures and Congress can now draft it from the bill catalog (OPUS-GOV, Oct 14).
why: The CTO ruled (October 14, 2026) that a public-salary base is a standing law at each level and asked dev mode's PR to add the data row and the smallest read hook, for the GOV wiring session to own after merge.
replacement: School districts as their own level of government, and the hiring engines (OPUS-WORLD) reading the floor when they set a new public hire's pay.

whatItFakes: How soon a body may undo a law it passed: no place's data records a reconsideration rule, so a sliding reluctance (fresher law and wider margin, more reluctance; a member's own last vote) stands in for the rule.
why: Laws stress audit defect 3 (Oct 14): a county repealed laws it passed two weeks earlier. The owner's exact rule is pending (CTO relay, Oct 14).
replacement: The owner's ruling on reconsideration, and each place's recorded rule as data where one exists. Resolved 2026-10-14: Owner ruling (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md): 'Repealing a fresh law: the body's own rules from data; where none, a sliding reluctance from how recently and by how much it passed. No fixed cooldown.' The reluctance is that rule (OPUS-GOV, Oct 14).

whatItFakes: A person without a seat asking a member they know to carry a bill, and the member's answer from their own position on it, their tie to the asker and the asker's standing; built ahead of the owner's confirmation.
why: Player-path audit (Oct 14): a player who lost an election should be able to ask a member to carry a bill. The CTO relayed it with owner confirmation pending.
replacement: The owner's confirmation of the carry request (or its replacement); then this row resolves. Resolved 2026-10-14: Owner ruling (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md, player-path audit, confirmed by the owner): a loser can 'ask a council member they know to carry a bill (the constituent path)'. The member decides by their own position and the asker's standing (OPUS-GOV, Oct 14).

whatItFakes: One national rule for how a mayor or county executive brings a bill of their own: through a member who carries it at their request. Charters differ (some let the mayor introduce ordinances directly).
why: No per-place charter data on executive bill introduction exists yet; the national pattern (NLC, NACo) stands in.
replacement: Research done Oct 23, 2026: each place's general-law default is in data/research/gov/local-executive-introduction-2026.json (all 56 places; 6 mayor rows SOURCED from the state statute or council rule, one of which seats the mayor on the council as a voting member; the rest ESTIMATED from the national pattern and data/research/local-government/county-governing-bodies.json), checked by scripts/research/legislature-local-rules-check.ts. proposalRight reading the place's row is the builder item gov-legislature-local-rules-by-place. Stays open: per-city and per-county charters are unread, and most rows are ESTIMATED.

whatItFakes: How much traits, ties, evidence, prominence, party, money and the prosecutor's record weigh at each step from a report to a sentence.
why: The small justice engine needs a first version; the research gives the directions (Gordon 2009 on partisan prosecution, the Justice Manual's charging standard, the Sentencing Guidelines), not these coefficients.
replacement: Weights checked against the Public Integrity Section's yearly counts of public-corruption charges and convictions by level of office, and against federal plea and trial-conviction shares.

whatItFakes: A state prosecutor's office where the offices data has neither a county prosecutor covering the town nor an elected attorney general.
why: Appointed attorneys general and territorial prosecutors are not in the offices data.
replacement: Appointed attorneys general and territorial attorneys general as offices in the offices data, with their appointing rule.

whatItFakes: Bribery is sentenced on the place's lowest felony-assault range from the sentencing research, not on the place's own bribery statute.
why: The sentencing research has not read bribery statutes yet (its campaign-funds row is unread in every place).
replacement: Each place's bribery-of-a-public-official grade and range read into data/research/justice/sentencing-ranges-2026.json, read by offense key. Oct 23, 2026 (research-gov-sourced-parameters): briberyRange in src/core2/justice-law.ts now reads each place's crime:bribery row; 43 places are read from their own statutes (official code sites; Arizona, New Hampshire and New York through the WebFetch reader) and sentenced on them, tagged SOURCED. Still estimated: 13 places whose code could not be fetched from the cloud take the mean of the 43 (8 to 98 months, ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE, each row's unreadReason naming the site and error); this stopgap closes when those statutes are read.

whatItFakes: Every place vacates an office on a felony conviction, on the day of the conviction, and forfeits all of a bribe's proceeds.
why: The common rule in state constitutions and codes; each state's rule and its timing (conviction, sentencing or final appeal) are not read.
replacement: Each state's forfeiture-of-office rule and timing, and its rule for forfeiting a bribe's proceeds, as data by state.

whatItFakes: The justice engine writes a prisoner's discretionary-choice flag on the person directly, because the core's updatePerson does not take it.
why: The core has no call for a module to take a person's own choices away for a time. Resolved by second Session D, 2026-10-15: updatePerson accepts the optional eligibility flag and clears it when explicitly undefined; custody and release use that API instead of direct person writes.
replacement: An OPUS-CORE call (updatePerson accepting discretionaryEligibleV1, or a custody hold) used by justice-custody.ts.

whatItFakes: The player's report and plea are decided by the character's own traits and the case's reads, like anyone else's, instead of being offered to the player.
why: The hearing scene has no choice wired to the plea yet; the small version plays the hearing and verdict as scenes only.
replacement: The plea and the report offered to the player as choices in the hearing scene, through the director.

whatItFakes: A job the jobs engine gives a person in prison is ended by the justice engine before its first shift, instead of the jobs engine never hiring them.
why: Resolved: jobs reads indexed custody before full or counted job search, applications and hiring, withdraws pending offers on imprisonment and rechecks acceptance. Staff candidates and the shared public payroll writer also read custody. Justice ends only jobs held when imprisonment begins; the daily repair is removed.
replacement: The jobs engine skips people in custody (justice's inCustody, or discretionaryEligibleV1 false) when deciding who looks for work and whom an employer hires.

whatItFakes: A convicted official keeps the bribe they took; the court collects only the fine.
why: The small justice engine sentences and fines; forfeiture of the proceeds (18 U.S.C. 981 and the states' forfeiture laws) is not built.
replacement: The bribe's amount forfeited from the official's cash to the treasury on the journal at sentencing, from each place's forfeiture law. Built Oct 15 (justice.ts convict): the bribe money the defendant took is forfeited first, then the fine; the per-place rule is SG-GOV-justice-forfeiture-by-place.

whatItFakes: Only the employers' group, formed against a wage bill, has a lobbyist who weighs a bribe; a bill that costs people money any other way draws no bribe, because its losses aren't measured per payer.
why: The only per-payer loss the engines measure today is a wage bill's (employerCosts). The CTO's next item, employer groups forming from who loses money on any bill, builds that measure.
replacement: One 'who loses money on this bill' reading over every provision kind, read by both employer groups and bribes. Resolved 2026-10-14: Employer groups now form over any bill that binds employers (employerStakes), and their lobbyist weighs a bribe at the first meeting; the remaining estimate is SG-GOV-bound-employer-cost-estimate (OPUS-GOV).

whatItFakes: An official who helps a resident looking for work refers them to the workforce office, but the jobs engine doesn't read the referral when employers pick applicants, so the help changes nothing yet.
why: The silent-engines audit (Oct 14) found constituent cases run but unread; the hiring read is the jobs engine's (OPUS-WORLD).
replacement: The jobs engine reads an official's referral as one of an applicant's reasons when an employer picks among them (OPUS-WORLD). Done Oct 16: recordReferral writes it and the weekly match adds jobsFitReferralWeight times its standing to the applicant's fit.

whatItFakes: What a policy costs each employer it binds is an estimated share of the employer's payroll (boundEmployerCostShare), except laws that price energy (clean electricity standard, carbon price), which cost each employer its own energy costs by the price engine's arithmetic. Other law-reach policies that bind employers record who is bound and move no money.
why: The CTO's item (Oct 14): employers organize from who loses money on any bill (the owner's Sept 26 ruling). Law-reach measures a money effect per employer only for the wage floor.
replacement: Each law-reach policy that binds employers moves its own money (a price, a fee, a compliance cost), and the stake reads that.

whatItFakes: One national bar on when a local recall may start (not in a term's first 180 days; not again in a term after one failed), not each state's own statute.
why: The owner's ruling (Oct 14): the recall rule reads the place's statute (grounds, signatures, cooling period). The municipal rule pack holds grounds, threshold and circulation window, but no cooling period yet.
replacement: Each state's recall timing bars read into the municipal rule pack and resolved like its threshold and window. Oct 23, 2026 (research-core-sourced-parameters): twelve more places read from statute (AK, DC, FL, GA, LA, MT, NE, NV, ND, SD, WA, WY; 5 SOURCED and 7 ESTIMATED: ND and WA where the bar counts from an election, FL where the bar is a fraction of the term, SG-GOV-recall-bars-term-fraction, and LA, MT, NE and NV where the bar is counted in calendar months and stored as days, SG-GOV-recall-bars-calendar-months) into src/core2/data/campaigns/recall-bars.json, read by recallBarsFor in src/core2/modules/recalls.ts, with the quotes and each state's bar after a failed recall in data/research/core/recall-timing-statutes-2026.json (checked by scripts/research/check-core-research.ts); 21 of the 22 places with a petitioned local recall now have a bar read from their own statute, seven of the twelve new ones estimates. Still open: no Mississippi timing bar was read, so the national estimate stands there; bars counted from an election (NE, WA, ND) and each state's rule after a failed recall wait on the builder item gov-recall-bars-election-clock.

whatItFakes: A recall bar that a statute counts in calendar months is stored in src/core2/data/campaigns/recall-bars.json as a fixed number of days: six months as 182 days (Louisiana's closing bar, Nebraska's and Nevada's opening bars, and the earlier Arizona and Oregon opening bars and California's closing bar) and two months as 61 days (Montana's opening bar). Six calendar months run 181 to 184 days and two run 59 to 62, depending on the date counted from, so the stored bar can admit a date the statute bars or bar one it admits by up to three days: for a term ending January 1, 2027, July 2, 2026 is inside six months but 183 days away, and Louisiana's 182-day bar admits it. Each of these rows is ESTIMATED with its spread.
why: The bar table and recallBarsFor count days into the term and days before its end; a calendar month has no fixed length in days, and counting by months changes engine logic, which is builder work, not research.
replacement: Builder item gov-recall-bars-calendar-months: a bar row may state calendar months (opening and closing), and the recall engine compares the date with the term's start plus those months, or its end less them, so the rows are SOURCED from their statute quotes. Until then they are ESTIMATED in src/core2/data/campaigns/recall-bars.json and data/research/core/recall-timing-statutes-2026.json, and scripts/research/check-core-research.ts recomputes each spread from the calendar.

whatItFakes: A recall bar that a statute sets as a fraction of the term (Florida: one-fourth of the term, Fla. Stat. 100.361(8)) is stored as two day counts: one for terms of up to longTermAboveYears years and one for longer terms. recallBarsFor returns the same 365 days for a three-year term as for a four-year term, 91 days more than one-fourth of three years (273.75 days), and about 183 days fewer than one-fourth of a six-year term (547.5 days). The row is ESTIMATED with a spread of 182 to 365 days, the statute's bar for terms of 2, 3 and 4 years. Today every Florida council, mayor and county commission seat takes four years, where the value is exact.
why: recall-bars.json holds days into the term, with one value per term band; every other bar in it is counted in days or months, so no row had to scale with the term until Florida's statute was read on Oct 23, 2026. Encoding a fraction of the term changes engine logic, which is builder work, not research.
replacement: Builder item gov-recall-bars-fraction-of-term: a bar row may state a fraction of the term, and recallBarsFor in src/core2/modules/recalls.ts turns it into days for the term at hand (term years x 365.25 x the fraction), so the row is SOURCED from the statute's own quote. Until then the row is ESTIMATED in src/core2/data/campaigns/recall-bars.json and data/research/core/recall-timing-statutes-2026.json, and scripts/research/check-core-research.ts checks that the statute's days for terms of 2, 3 and 4 years fall inside its spread.

whatItFakes: Every town's and county's body numbers its ordinances the same way, by the year and order of introduction ("2026-12"), and opens them with the same 'Be it ordained by' clause, not each place's own style.
why: The owner's ruling (Oct 14): bills follow the real form of their body. States and Congress have recorded numbering and enacting clauses; local bodies' styles are not in the data yet.
replacement: Research done Oct 23, 2026: the enacting clause and numbering each place's general law gives are in data/research/gov/local-ordinance-style-2026.json (all 56 places; 12 municipal clauses, 2 county clauses and one council's two-part numbering SOURCED from statute or rule; no state statute read sets an ordinance numbering, so elsewhere numbering keeps the national pattern, ESTIMATED), checked by scripts/research/legislature-local-rules-check.ts. bodyNumbering reading the place's row is gov-legislature-local-rules-by-place; the clause wording is the Words item words-local-enacting-clause-by-state. Stays open: charter towns keep their own style (their code of ordinances is the record), and most rows are ESTIMATED.

whatItFakes: Every state chamber and Congress keeps the same nine subject committees (finance, judiciary, education, health, labor and commerce, transportation, environment, housing, government), not its own list and names.
why: The audit found every bill going to one 'general' committee. Each chamber's own committee list is not in the data yet; the nine subjects are the ones nearly every chamber keeps.
replacement: Each chamber's standing committees and the subjects they hear, read from its rules (Book of the States Table 3.23 and each chamber's committee page), the way Congress's are in data/office-day/federal-committees.json.

whatItFakes: The civilian board costs the city a yearly amount per resident and is recorded against the police department, but no complaint against an officer is brought or reviewed.
why: No engine records a police-stop complaint, a board finding or officer discipline; the board's cost and its department are built.
replacement: GOV: the justice engine files a resident's complaint against an officer from a police stop and the board reviews it, its finding read by the department's discipline.

whatItFakes: Young adults are recorded as heard in juvenile court, but their cases still go to adult court.
why: Session A checked main: justice sentencing has no adult-versus-juvenile court-routing record. An age-labeled reach row cannot change a hearing or sentence. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records adult-versus-juvenile court routing; the justice engine hears only corruption cases.
replacement: GOV: the justice engine reads the juvenile age in force when it routes a defendant's case, and the sentence follows that court's range.
resolution: The engine routes each arrested person's case to juvenile or adult court by the juvenile age in force, and the sentence and cost follow that court (src/core2/public-safety.ts).

whatItFakes: A permit requirement is recorded on adults and the sheriff, but no one applies for, holds or is refused a permit.
why: Session A checked main: there is no carried-weapon or permit application record. Legal reach on an adult does not establish possession, an application or a permit decision. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records a carried weapon, a permit application or a permit decision.
replacement: GOV with OPUS-PEOPLE: the justice engine reads the permit law when a carried weapon is part of a case, and the sheriff's office issues permits.
resolution: Adults in gun-owning households apply for, hold and renew permits, paying the state fee and the class through the journal; adults under 21 are refused (src/core2/public-safety.ts).

whatItFakes: A purchase age is recorded on dealers and young adults, but no handgun sale is made or refused.
why: Session A checked main: purchases are aggregate money flows with no handgun sale or buyer-age check. Applying an age to every young adult would invent an attempted purchase. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records a handgun sale or a buyer-age check.
replacement: OPUS-WORLD: the business engine's sales read the purchase age when a store sells to a person.
resolution: Young adults in gun-owning households buy handguns from private sellers where no age limit applies and are refused where one does (src/core2/public-safety.ts).

whatItFakes: The rule is recorded on adults, but no self-defense case is charged or decided under it.
why: Session A checked main: justice has no self-defense incident or charging claim with retreat facts. A law row cannot establish those facts for an arbitrary defendant. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records a self-defense incident or a charging decision on one; the justice engine hears only corruption cases.
replacement: GOV: the prosecutor's charging decision and the court read the law in force when a case turns on self-defense.
resolution: Self-defense claims in assault cases end at charging where the rule is law, and only those with no safe retreat end there where the duty to retreat applies (src/core2/public-safety.ts).

whatItFakes: Small employers (under 20 staff, outside the federal age law) weigh older applicants down where no ban is law, and a ban removes it (jobs-age-bias.ts); the world records no other protected trait (race, orientation, disability) and no applicant pool for rentals, so landlords' leases do not read the ban and no complaint is brought.
why: People carry a gender and a birth date but no other protected trait, and the housing engine leases to any homeless household that meets the income multiple with no applicants to choose among.
replacement: Record protected traits for people and counted groups, give rentals an applicant pool the landlord chooses from reading the ban, and let a refused applicant bring a complaint the justice engine hears.

whatItFakes: The restriction raises counted births through the outcome web's birth-rate factor (births-counted.ts records the counted women it applied to); full women's planned pregnancies and the cost of an extra birth (a newborn's living cost is zero) do not read it, and no termination or denial is recorded.
why: Full pregnancies come from agreed family plans, there is no unplanned pregnancy or termination request, and a counted newborn carries no living cost.
replacement: OPUS-PEOPLE: the renewal engine models unplanned pregnancies and the woman's decision, reading the law where she lives, the distance to a provider and her reasons; newborns carry a living cost.

whatItFakes: Telecommunications businesses (online platforms and internet providers) with an operating cost base pay a share of their other operating costs to verify new accounts (business.ts, monthly), whether or not they employ anyone in the town; minors' account opening, parental consent and refusals are not recorded.
why: No minor account-opening or consent record exists; the cost is an estimated share of operating costs, not a count of verifications.
replacement: OPUS-PEOPLE: a teenager's media use and a parent's consent read the law, and the platforms' cost follows the accounts verified.

whatItFakes: The police line rises by an estimated oversight share (reporting, policy and court-order work) under the restriction, paid by the treasury; no investigation uses or is barred from facial recognition.
why: Justice investigations have witness, hearsay and payment evidence but no facial-identification request or warrant record.
replacement: GOV: the justice engine's identification of a suspect reads the rule and needs a warrant where it applies.

whatItFakes: Rights are recorded on residents, but no request to see or delete data is made. The compliance cost is now read by the business engine (every employing business in town pays a share of its operating costs while the law is in force), but the law's coverage thresholds (revenue, number of consumers) are not modeled, so it falls on every employing business alike.
why: Session A checked main: no customer-data holdings or access/deletion request exists. The business engine's monthly cost review now reads the law (readBusinessDuty in src/core2/modules/business.ts); what a request is, and which businesses hold enough data to be covered, have no records.
replacement: PEOPLE with WORLD: a resident's request to see or delete data, answered by a business that holds customer data; coverage thresholds from the statute's terms read per business.

whatItFakes: Broader local power is recorded on the town and its council, but the authority check still reads only the specific grants.
why: Session A checked main: legislature.authorityFor returns specific wage/tax grants and policy preemptions; otherwise it already permits local policy questions. There is no undecided authority category whose permission a broader grant would change. A read returning the same result would not prove an effect.
replacement: GOV: authorityFor reads home rule in force as a grant for any question the state hasn't decided.
resolvedBy: Claude (laws-record-only-reads), Oct 15: policyAuthority (src/core2/policy-authority.ts) already reads the state's home-rule law for every question the powers catalog leaves open for a city; it was proven only by a hand-inserted fixture. src/core2/home-rule-played.test.ts now shows, in a generated town, a council's draft of such an ordinance blocked with the grant repealed, drafted once the state's grant takes effect (the bill's authority row cites the grant's law id), and blocked again on repeal.

whatItFakes: A member with no person record (a seat held by no one filled in) is present at every vote; every other member decides from their own day.
why: The audit found nobody ever absent. A member without a person record has no day, health or temperament to miss a vote from.
replacement: Every seat's holder filled in as a person before they vote, so attendance reads their day like anyone's. Done Oct 16: a seat whose holder has no living person record casts no vote and moves no pill, so the stand-in is gone.

whatItFakes: A member with no person record never moves a poison pill; every other member decides from their own temperament.
why: A member without a person record has no traits for the chooser to read.
replacement: Every seat's holder filled in as a person before they vote, so floor tactics read their temperament like anyone's. Done Oct 16: a seat whose holder has no living person record casts no vote and moves no pill, so the stand-in is gone.

whatItFakes: A municipal collective whose listing name gives no kind of municipality (no "CITY OF", "TOWN OF", "VILLAGE OF" or "BOROUGH OF") and whose government the game has not compiled is named after the town and "Council"; a compiled town's body takes the name its charter gives it, and any other town the usual body of its kind in its state (municipalByState and municipalByKind in the same file).
why: Only the 144 compiled municipal governments carry a charter reading; every other town's charter is unread. Narrowed Oct 19: the compiled readers now carry the body name. Narrowed again: a town of a listed kind takes its state's usual body, so only the few consolidated governments listed by bare name keep the generic name.
replacement: Carry each charter’s collective body name into the municipal reading and replace the default.

whatItFakes: Until jurisdiction-specific dual-office exceptions are compiled, the data conservatively treats two elected mandates as incompatible. The federal legislative/executive prohibition is sourced separately.
why: The repository has no per-place dual-office compilation; the previous engine vacated every prior office without reading any law. Research endpoint returned a web application firewall block.
replacement: Source each place’s prohibitions and exceptions, replacing the estimated pairs in the same reader.

whatItFakes: A question with no mapping in the powers catalog, or a local question whose gating state law is not on record, cannot be introduced; the authority result records a disputed missing grant rather than silently permitting the action. (Oct 15: a territory's cell the catalog has not read now takes its state cell, an estimate; see SG-GOV-policy-power-conditions.)
why: All 59 policy questions are mapped. What remains unresolved is a gating state law not yet recorded, which the engine cannot infer from absent research.
replacement: The gating state laws recorded in the opening law table for every place, read before introduction and executive orders.

whatItFakes: Inherited game-profile powers cells are provisional estimates; a cell explicitly marked limited retains a disputed grant while its qualitative conditions are not yet all executable predicates. A territory's unread cell is its state cell (data/research/powers-catalog/territory-grant.json), an estimate.
why: The shared research catalog includes unsourced game-profile cells and records some conditional powers in prose rather than structured constraints.
replacement: Sourced per-place cells and structured conditions for each limited power, evaluated by the same authority reader before introduction or an executive order. Researched Oct 23, 2026 (research-core-sourced-parameters): NACo Research (2022) county authority by state (a level from 1, Dillon's Rule, to 6, home rule, with the home rule option and Dillon's Rule flexibilities) for all 56 places in data/research/core/naco-2022-county-authority.json, the per-place input for the county cells whose condition is home rule or Dillon's Rule. Still open: no limited cell's condition is an executable predicate yet; the builder item core-policy-authority-limited-cell-predicates reads the file in src/core2/policy-authority.ts. Territory cells stay with laws-territory-powers-research.

whatItFakes: Background Congress uses the shared platform question pool, which lacks most federal-only questions in the powers catalog. Only supported questions with federal scope can be proposed; state-specific questions no longer stand in for federal policy.
why: Federal-only policy questions need recorded starting answers, official stances and downstream effect readers before adding them to the shared proposal pool.
replacement: Wire the federal-only questions through the existing stance, law and effect engines, with named-person played-world evidence, then include them in the proposal pool.

whatItFakes: Repealing a starting graduated income-tax schedule uses the existing estimated state or local flat rate. The binary catalog provision carries no replacement rate, deduction or filing-status rules.
why: Tax Foundation's 2025 state survey and actual conversion laws have distinct enacted rates and deductions. The catalog's Boolean question cannot supply those terms. Received explanation and director acceptance remain unproven.
replacement: Explicit replacement tax terms in the provision: the sponsor writes the flat rate (and keeps or changes the zero bracket and standard deduction) as the legislature's rate sections already do (shapedRate in src/core2/modules/legislature.ts), read by incomeTaxAct and the withholding engine for full and counted workers, with a received explanation and director line for an affected worker (builder item laws-income-tax-flatten-sponsor-rate). Oct 23, 2026: the band it reads is sourced in data/research/laws/taxfoundation-2022-2026-flat-tax-conversions.json (Tax Foundation, January 1 tables 2022-2026: five real conversions chose 0.667 to 1.0 of the old top rate, median 0.786; the 14 flat-rate states of January 1, 2025 run 2.5% to 5.695%, median 4.25%, now the ESTIMATED stateFlatIncomeTaxPercent in src/core2/data/laws/reach-group-b-parameters.json, checked by scripts/research/check-law-reach-sources.ts).

whatItFakes: A council seat chosen by part of town counts only the voters of its part: the town's households in their recorded order are cut into equal runs, one per seat chosen that way, and the counted residents and the rest of the town divide equally among them. No part of town has a boundary or a street behind it.
why: The world holds no street map or address inside a town, and no record of how a place's council districts or wards are drawn.
replacement: Council districts drawn from the town's dwellings (by the council or a commission, to near equal population as its charter says), each household and each sitting member placed by their dwelling.

whatItFakes: A candidate for a council seat chosen by part of town must live in that part of town. The rule is assumed for every place: no charter text the repository holds says whether its ward or district seats ask it, and the part of town is the household-order ward of SG-GOV-ward-map.
why: The compiled charters (src/core2/gov-rules/municipal-governments.json) carry only the council's composition, and governing-body-seat-qualification.json only the minimum age; most ward and district charters do ask residency in the ward, but no place's own text has been read.
replacement: Read each place's charter or state law for whether a ward or district candidate must live in it, and apply the check only where it does; the part of town then comes from the dwellings, as SG-GOV-ward-map's replacement draws it.

whatItFakes: Where a place has no researched failure-to-elect row for an office family, the holdover rule is the family estimate (data/offices/holdover.json). Repeat special elections are dated by the state's special-election rule or its estimate. National presidential failure-to-elect is not implemented.
why: Existing vacancy data governs filling a vacancy but does not establish when failure to elect creates one. Only congressional fixed term boundaries are sourced here.
replacement: A researched failure-to-elect row for each of the 56 places and each office family, and the national presidential contingent-election path.

whatItFakes: Wider races reach named officials across their jurisdiction and the played town residents: a state race, the state's officials and serving holders; a national race, every member of Congress, the town's own state's officials and every place's governor and statewide officers (another place's are filled in from their term rows the first time a national pool is built, fillStatewideHolders in src/core2/candidate-pool.ts), but not another place's legislators, who stay named on their terms (SG-GOV-outside-legislators-national-pool). Unnamed ordinary residents elsewhere have no candidate records. State legislative district residency is not individually known for officials stored at state scope.
why: The wider electorate has counts but no resident household records from which candidacy can read personal resources and ambitions.
replacement: Jurisdiction-wide counted household records with district membership, using the same candidacy reasons before filling in a runner.

whatItFakes: Uses the CTO ruling that working press staff and outlet owners cannot run for office while retaining that role.
why: OWNER-DECISIONS.md records the October 14, 2026 ruling as pending owner confirmation.
replacement: Owner confirmation or revision of the press-employment conflict rule; apply the chosen rule to all candidate filing paths. Done Oct 19 (gov-press-ban-withdrawn): the owner withdrew the ban on Oct 16 ("a reporter who wants to run may run"; OWNER-DECISIONS). The press-employment check is gone from checkEligibility, the candidacy chooser and the candidate pool, so press staff file and run like anyone; only the automatic vacancy stand-in still passes over press jobs, because the defect was a reporter seated without an election.

whatItFakes: A contest filed with a state or territory election board, commission or division (not the secretary of state) names no clerk: the filing scene shows the office's title with no one at the counter.
why: The state election agencies are titles in the filing data; no record lists their staff, and a board has no single holder to name.
replacement: Resolved Oct 16: the executive engine seats a chief election official for the state (appointment post chief-election-official), a full person on the state payroll, and the filing clerk returns them (pool item gov-state-election-office-holder).

whatItFakes: Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Marianas and the U.S. Virgin Islands have no legislative-district geography or member roster in the data, so each chamber's recorded seats are all elected at large by the whole territory.
why: The Census Gazetteer legislative districts cover the states, D.C. and Puerto Rico only; the territories' own districts (Guam at large, the Virgin Islands by island, the Northern Marianas by island and village, American Samoa's counties and districts) are not yet read.
replacement: Each territory's districts and sitting members, read from the territory's election commission, so seats are elected by district and hold the real parties and names.

whatItFakes: A home the government-units listing ties to no local government (a place outside any organized borough, a census place inside a consolidated city-county or city-parish government, a newer census place the place-to-county relation misses) has no local office, so the player's first race there is the state's own lawmaking body instead of the place's council or its equivalent.
why: The owner's Oct 29 ruling gives every place a first local race under whatever name its lawmaking body has; 244 of the 32,350 state localities have no local office in the data (src/core2/player-first-race.test.ts prints the ones it draws) because placeLocalGovernmentUnits finds no government unit serving them. The District of Columbia is not one: its council and mayor sit at the state level. The island areas' villages are their territories' own case.
replacement: Each such home matched to the government that serves it (the borough, or the state where no borough is organized; the consolidated city-county or city-parish; the county the relation misses), so localOfficesForPlace seats its council or equivalent and the rule admits it.

whatItFakes: A body with committees takes a scheduled bill to its committee a week ahead of the floor, and the committee decides on its own day without the pre-vote hooks that run on the floor day: staff briefings, interest groups organizing, public comment and the player's own vote. Whether any of them belong to the committee day (a public comment at the committee's hearing, a briefing before a committee vote) is the owner's call.
why: Moving the committee off the floor day split it from the hooks that run just before a vote. The simplest version keeps every hook on the floor day, as before, so nothing already built changes order.
replacement: The owner's ruling on which pre-vote hooks run on the committee day (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md).
resolution: The committee's day runs whatever the records already fire for a body on a sitting day, at the stage the body's own rules put them, from data. The pre-vote hooks are named (staff-brief, interest-organize, public-comment, own-vote); src/core2/data/legislature/committee-day.json says which run at the committee stage, holdCommittee runs those before the committee decides and marks them on the bill (hooksRun), and the floor day runs only those not yet run.

whatItFakes: In a state where a board, council or senate holds or must concur in clemency (board alone, board with the governor, governor with a board's recommendation, a council's or the senate's consent), the governor's day has no clemency act: the board's own decisions are not simulated, so no prisoner is released there by clemency.
why: The governor decides alone only where the state's law says so (governor alone, or a board that only advises); the other authorities need a board or council engine that does not exist yet.
replacement: A clemency board engine (members, petitions, recommendations) and the council or senate consent, read by the governor's act where the law requires it.

whatItFakes: Posted bail goes into the prosecuting government's general treasury cash, so the treasury can spend it before the trial and hand back only what it still holds; the shortfall is recorded on the return, not escrowed.
why: The journal has no court fund or escrow account to set bail aside; adding one is a new account kind under the treasury's owner.
replacement: A court escrow fund account that holds each bail apart from spendable treasury cash, returned in full at disposition.
resolution: Bail now sits in a court escrow account under the prosecuting treasury's owner (account:<treasury>:court-escrow), apart from its spendable cash, and the trial returns the whole bail from it.

whatItFakes: An island area's state-level government has no spending or revenue by function in the data (Census state finances cover the states and D.C.). Its budget takes the states' residents-weighted function mix, scaled to the area's own all-funds spending a resident where published (Guam, the Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico) and to the median of those where not (American Samoa, the Northern Marianas), with revenue equal to spending.
why: public-budget-bases.json holds an all-funds total for three island areas and no breakdown for any; without a budget its treasury is empty and its officials and agencies cannot be paid.
replacement: Each island area's published budget by function and its revenue by source (Guam, Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico budget documents; American Samoa and the Northern Marianas' Office of Insular Affairs financial reports) in public-budget-bases.json.

whatItFakes: A campaign walks the town's doors oldest household first, then by id. Each evening opens as many doors as the knocked homes' readiness adds up to, so the order decides who is reached first, not whether a street of younger homes is reached at all.
why: Added when only older residents could open the door (New Baltimore, Ohio: 45 doors, none opened under an id-ordered walk). Whether a walk list follows age, turnout history, party or the street is the owner's call; the acting CTO kept this order (Oct 24) until the campaigns engine reads a route from the map.
