replacement: The owner's ruling on how a campaign orders the doors it knocks (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md), built as the campaign's own choice of list.

whatItFakes: A government's charges and fees follow its budget's charges line; no council or legislature bill sets a fee's level (a transit fare, a park fee), so a player cannot raise one by bill.
why: Whether councils set fees by bill is the owner's call: a real-world step the game lacks is a question, not a feature (DECISION-REGISTER, Oct 14). Asked in OWNER-DECISIONS.md, Open.
replacement: The owner's ruling: either the charges line stays the budget's, or a fee-schedule provision on a bill that the budget's charges line and the households' payments read. (pool item gov-fee-level-by-bill).

whatItFakes: A counted voter weighing a recall over misconduct, or the member's answer to the petition at the due day's count, reads the share of the town's named adults who heard of it as their own exposure, since counted residents keep no record of the stories they heard.
why: The news engine records who heard a story only for named people; the counted population has no hearing record of its own.
replacement: A per-group hearing record for counted residents, kept by the news engine, that the recall reads like a named voter's.

whatItFakes: A small town's appointed department heads work a full-time public-office week at a cut hourly rate (a Prescott, Michigan planning director at $1.07 an hour for 8.5 hours) when their budget line carries only a part-time stipend. The pay in total matches the line; the hours and the hourly rate do not. The minimum wage skips these posts by law (data/laws/minimum-wage-exempt.json), so a wage raise no longer multiplies their pay.
why: The work schedule a post follows is a template's full-time slots, and the payroll pays the hourly rate for the minutes scheduled; fitting hours to a stipend needs a part-time schedule for the post.
replacement: A post whose line carries less than a full-time week takes a part-time schedule sized to the stipend at the going rate (Census ASPEP part-time municipal payroll), so its hours and hourly rate both match the source.

whatItFakes: An ask to the player to carry a bill is held as a request (the carryAsks table) and answered by answerCarryAsk, but no bench screen shows it or has Agree and Decline controls, so in play the player can never answer it and the ask never closes.
why: The bench's Politics screens belong to the play-first lane; the engine side (the held ask, the answer that files the bill with the player as sponsor and the asker as requestedBy) is built and tested, and the screen is the lane's.
replacement: A waiting ask on Politics, Issues and Government, with Agree and Decline controls wired to answerCarryAsk, reading carryAsksAwaiting (pool item gov-carry-ask-player-decides).

whatItFakes: A state's or county's rent-help line is paid to the played town by the town's share of the government's population, as though renter households were spread the same way as people.
why: Renter households are not recorded for the whole government, only for the played town, so the town's slice of a larger government's line cannot be read from renters; the population share is the nearest record that exists.
replacement: Record renter households per government (counted, as the town's are) and pay each line by the town's share of them; the stopgap clears when the share reads renters.

whatItFakes: A member of a body who is a named official not yet filled in as a full person (many state and federal members) is never recorded as voting a contract to a firm they or their family own, because the records hold no kin or firm for them until they are filled in; only full people can hold a conflict of interest.
why: Named officials outside the player's circle carry no family or business records until the player meets or clicks them, and the contracts engine weighs their ties as none for the same reason.
replacement: When an official is filled in, the family and firms they were generated with are read by the same familyRelation read, and the vote is checked against the winning firm's owner then; a firm owned by a counted or outside owner reads through the owner's recorded kin the same way.

whatItFakes: Whoever fills a seat the offices engine keeps no term for (another state's member of Congress, whom the officials engine seats from the roster) sits in the party of the one they replace: an appointee or a special election's winner is assumed to keep the seat's party. Since gov-every-state-and-town-governs U1 (Oct 29) every other place's chambers, governor and statewide executives are held on office terms, so their vacancies go through the offices engine's own fill, not this one.
why: The officials engine seats other states' members of Congress without the offices engine's terms, so no record names the appointee or the special election's candidates.
replacement: Other states' seats in Congress held on office terms like every other seat, so the appointing authority's choice or the special election's result (the voting engine's world races) names the holder and their party.

whatItFakes: Where a place's filing row in data/research/elections/filing-requirements.json gives its signature rule as a formula (for example a share of the votes cast for the office at its last election: 27 municipal, 21 county, 14 state legislative, 13 statewide and 13 U.S. House party rows) or gives nothing, the filing's petition asks the median of the read counts for its office family and side (an independents' row that is not its own reads the party row): for a party filing 28 municipal, 50 county, 113 state legislative, 2,000 statewide and 500 U.S. House; for an independent 30, 25, 125, 3,501 and 1,000.
why: The formulas are kept as free text; no structured threshold (share, base, minimum and maximum) is read for them yet.
replacement: A structured threshold for each formula row, its base read from the world's own results through the recall engine's signatureBase (src/core2/modules/recalls.ts), the median kept only where a row gives nothing.

whatItFakes: Where a contest's district reaches past the town (a county seat drawn as a state's places, a legislative, U.S. House or statewide race), the clerk counts the town's share of the law's signatures, by the town's eligible voters over the district's, at least one: the signatures a candidate would gather in the places the world holds only as counts are neither gathered nor checked.
why: The world holds people one by one only in the town (two-level population); a canvass, an event and a circle reach only the town.
replacement: Signatures gathered in the district's other places at a coarse step, from the campaign's effort there, checked against the law's whole count.

whatItFakes: Every other state's, D.C.'s and each territory's chambers, governor and statewide executives are seated at the opening as named officials on office terms, and each state's and D.C.'s legislators, governor and partisan statewide officers are raced on their own calendars (a territory's are not: SG-GOV-territory-legislature-race; nor is an office elected without party labels: SG-GOV-outside-nonpartisan-race), but only Congress and the town's own state legislature sit: no other legislature opens a session, files a bill or enacts a law.
why: gov-every-state-and-town-governs is built in units (docs/reports/world-governing-plan-2026-10-29.md): U1 seats every chamber; each body's law must be its own (U2) before another state's act can be written without landing as the town's own state law.
replacement: U3 of the plan: openWorldLegislating opens a session for Congress and every place in the session calendar data, each body voting from its members' saved positions on the official rows, never filling them in. The reads that fill a named holder in today (each calls holderOf) and must not run for an outside body in U3: legislature.ts members() and everything that reads a body through it (floor votes, committees and leadership.ts organize, staff, meetings, interest-groups lobbied, office-day, world-legislating chamber()), legislature.ts tieBreaker (the lieutenant governor) and executiveOf (the governor's signature or veto), and election-ties.ts bodyVotes; office-day-state.ts computerGovernorsDay already skips another place's offices (isOutsideOffice in offices.ts, by jurisdiction).

whatItFakes: A territory's legislative seats, governor and statewide executive seats outside the town (Puerto Rico's, Guam's, the Virgin Islands', American Samoa's and the Northern Marianas') are not raced, in the world races or a legislative special election, so their opening holders serve on past the elections their law holds (Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and the U.S. Virgin Islands elect a governor in November 2026); a legislative vacancy there is filled by the offices engine's stand-in.
why: The territories have no counted electorate places (no presidential vote or county places on record), so no count could decide a seat; several of their seats carry no party or a party of their own (Puerto Rico's New Progressive and Popular Democratic, American Samoa's nonpartisan Fono), not the two major parties the count fields. Without the skip each such race named no winner and the seat was never refilled.
replacement: Each territory's electorate places from its own legislative, executive or delegate results, and its own parties on the count, so its seats are raced on the same counted engine (the same replacement as SG-GOV-territory-governor-race).

whatItFakes: Another place's statewide office elected without party labels (about ten: superintendents of public instruction in California, North Dakota, Washington and Wisconsin, Oregon's labor commissioner, Hawaii's Office of Hawaiian Affairs trustees, D.C.'s state board of education president, Guam's public auditor and utilities commission, the Northern Marianas board of education) is seated at the opening but never raced, so its holder serves past the end of the term on its row.
why: The world races count two major parties' candidates; an office whose ballot carries no party labels (data/research/offices/unrecorded-holder-parties-2026.json, appliesTo office) has no partisan race to count, and the voting engine has no nonpartisan count for a race the town doesn't vote in.
replacement: A nonpartisan count for a race the town doesn't vote in (the incumbent against a challenger drawn from the state, decided by the places' votes on the candidates' own standing), so the seat loop in racesIn races these offices like every other.

whatItFakes: Another place's statewide officer whom the law elects on one ticket with the governor (a lieutenant governor in about thirty places, data/research/offices/state-offices.json electedWithGovernorOnTicket) is raced on its own seat, the same as every other statewide officer, so the count can seat a lieutenant governor of a different party from the governor elected the same night.
why: The world races count one seat at a time; nothing joins a ticket office's race to its governor's. The town's own contests run each office separately too.
replacement: A ticket office's race decided with its governor's: the governor race's winning party seats the running mate the same day, read from the office's research row.

whatItFakes: Another place's holder whose party neither the legislative roster nor the research (data/research/offices/unrecorded-holder-parties-2026.json) reads sits with no party on the term: six vacant legislative seats with no Ballotpedia vacancy row (Florida, Massachusetts, Missouri, New York), Guam's attorney general and the Virgin Islands board of elections (eight seats). Filled in as a person (holderOf in src/core2/modules/officials.ts), such a holder keeps the term's no party, so the person matches the term row, never the 2024 state-lean estimate. A race for such a seat fields both major parties as if it were open.
why: The research file lists them as unread seats; nothing on record names the holder's party.
replacement: Each seat's holder read into the research file (the chamber's own member page or the territory's election results), so seatOutsideOffices seats them in their party.

whatItFakes: A national race's pool (the presidency) holds every member of Congress, the town's own state's legislators and every place's governor and statewide officers, but not another place's legislators (about 7,400 seats): they are named officials on their term rows (personId null, the CTO's ruling of Oct 29, 22:40), and the pool weighs only full people, so none of them weighs running for president. Before U1 an 8-member sample of each other chamber, full people, stood in for them.
why: The chooser (decideToRun) reads a person's traits, money and party, which a named official on a term row does not have, and filling about 7,400 legislators in as full people to weigh one race would make people the player never meets (the two-level rule).
replacement: Another place's legislators weighed from their term rows by the same reasons as a full official (the seat's reach, the party's backing, an ambition read from the seat), the way candidacy's counted screen weighs counted residents, and filled in only when one runs.

whatItFakes: Every state seat the world races outside the town (each other place's legislators, governor and statewide officers, and the town's own state's districts that do not cover it; thousands of seats in an even year) keeps, every cycle, its race row, its count's results and places, the ended term beside the new one and the took-office record, and nothing folds the old ones once play no longer reads them. In Long Hill, Connecticut (seed m7b, four played years to January 2029) the offices engine's terms grow from 21,136 rows to 33,973 (main at the branch's base: 644 to 1,044), and the voting engine's races, results and returns from 185 to 13,932 rows each and its places from 624 to 40,981; November 2026 alone races 6,923 seats (Leola, South Dakota, seed m2-nov1). The took-office records themselves are not kept in the town's log (they are placed in the office's own place).
why: A fold needs each reader's window agreed with the session that owns that reader (the CTO's ruling of Oct 30, 04:14: the person card's past offices, the press's took-office story, the trace's record search), which this change cannot do; the Oct 30 01:55 records bar (years 97 to 100 at most 1.2 times years 1 to 4) is not yet measured for these tables.
replacement: A fold of each outside seat's ended terms, race rows and results older than its last few cycles into one summary row per seat (who held it, in which party, from and to), its readers' windows named, proven by a long save's records kept (pool item core-long-run-tables-grow-with-history).

whatItFakes: A world candidate whose newest record of the race is word of a rival's message (an ad, a mailer or an evening of doors; a rivalWord row) reads where their race stands as how warm the people they know in town are to that rival against how warm they are to them (each impression's warmth, none where cold or unreached, averaged over the circle): their circle's actual warmth to both, not what those people said to the candidate.
why: The campaigns engine keeps who told a candidate of a rival's message, but no record of what the people a candidate talks to say about the race; the circle's warmth is the nearest existing record of who they lean to. Recognition would not do: everyone in the circle knows the candidate, and an incumbent's have as a rule all heard of them, so it would never show a rival gaining.
replacement: A record of what the people a candidate talks to tell them about the race (who they have heard of, who they lean to), read by raceReading in place of the circle's recognition.

whatItFakes: A world candidate who campaigns harder because they know a rival stands ahead (an incumbent coming home to campaign) is kept as a steppedUp row and a campaign-stepped-up event, and the extra doors and hours reach voters, but no scene, journal line or news story tells it yet.
why: The words session writes the director's scenes from records the engines keep; the record lands first so the scene can name it by id.
replacement: The director's scene or news line of a candidate stepping up their campaign, read from the campaign-stepped-up event and its steppedUp row by id (words session).

whatItFakes: A town hall's room, a candidate's forum among them, fills only from the town's full adults (townHallDrives reads townAdults): a resident still in the counted wider population never comes, so a forum in a town of mostly counted residents meets only the people already filled in.
why: The forum (campaign-day.ts) reuses the meetings engine's one audience rule rather than a second one, and that rule was written before the counted tier; public comment already reads counted residents by the same drive (commentSpeakers) and fills in those who speak.
replacement: townHallDrives reads the town's counted adults by the same drive as commentSpeakers does (countedResidents with countedRecordOnly), indexed by place so a weekly town hall does not scan the whole wider population, and holdTownHall fills in each counted resident who comes before the room's causes are written.

whatItFakes: Donors outside the town (askOutsideDonors, for seats wider than the town) give only the savings share of the person rule (donationShareOfCashPerWarmth), and on a typical donor's whole account balance one for one (medianTransactionBalance at outsideDonorIncomeUsd), not as a named donor does on the savings beyond a cushion of their living costs, weighed on a log scale of that cushion; the share of a month's income after bills that a named donor also gives from (giftBudget, donationShareOfMonthPerWarmth, weighed on a log scale of donationMonthScaleMonths of their living costs) is not read for them.
why: The outside donor is a counted place group with no household of its own: no recorded monthly living costs to take from a typical donor's income, so the month's budget after bills cannot be read from records yet.
replacement: Read a typical donor household's monthly living costs for the place group (the same living-cost tables the population is built from), make the cushion and the month's spare from them, and give by donationAnswer's two log-scaled shares, so outside and named donors use one rule; recheck the outside share of a campaign's receipts against localInPlaceDonorShare (0.65, 0.25 to 0.95).

whatItFakes: A donor whose household holds no recorded living costs at all (no member carries a livingCostDailyMinor) has no span to weigh money against (weighedAgainst), so the month's spare after taxes and their savings each count one for one toward a gift, as if a dollar weighed the same however many they had, and their cushion is zero; the month's part is still capped at the month's spare. A donor with no living costs of their own but a household that has them already takes the span and cushion from their share of the household's month (giftBudget). In the calibration's drawn places these donors are press staff seated by identity fill-in (SG-PEOPLE-press-staff-households): 631 of 10,990 gifts but 44.6% of the money (408 places, 51 run seeds, Nov 1), $1,200 at the median and up to $5,049.
why: The opening population puts a household's living costs on its heads (population.ts), and the press module seats staff it cannot draw from the town's people alone, with no rent or living costs (SG-PEOPLE-press-staff-households), so their households hold none. Unknown costs are not zero, but nothing yet gives those households a month of costs, and the campaigns engine is not the place to price a household.
replacement: Give such households their month of living costs where they are made (press staff through the one-person household official-living.ts already gives owners and officials, giveLivingCost, or the household draw SG-PEOPLE-press-staff-households names), delete the one-for-one branch, and refit donationShareOfMonthPerWarmth: with those donors weighed against their town's median month instead, the best share (about 2.2) leaves 13% of eight-place and 3.3% of sixteen-place pools outside a band, so the money rule needs more than a new share.

whatItFakes: A bill's paper words the lawyer's warning on a disputed power as the body's lawyer, named by the body (bill-paper.authority.disputed-body), wherever no appointment gives the lawyer's title: a county board's bill (the executive engine seats only the town's departments at the opening, so the County Attorney post in executive-powers-2026.json is never filled), a township board's or a state chamber's bill, an unincorporated place, and a town whose City Attorney post is unfilled (the player's own post waiting for their choice, or nobody to appoint). A bill before the town's council names the town's own City Attorney appointment instead.
why: The register rules that the city attorney warns the player on a disputed power (DECISION-REGISTER, "A law changes the record first", Sept 22); the executive engine appoints a City Attorney for the town's council (appointTownDepartments) but no attorney or counsel for a county board, a township board or a legislature, and no title is typed in code.
replacement: The executive engine seats each other body's own lawyer as an appointment the way it seats the town's City Attorney (the county attorney from the county forms in executive-powers-2026.json, township counsel and legislative counsel from research on who advises each kind of body), and the paper names that appointment's title in bill-paper.authority.disputed.

whatItFakes: A candidate choosing which questions to run on reads the true share of the town's electorate on their side of each question (electorateSides: every named adult at their own view, every counted record at its record's stance times the people it stands for, by the stance the ballot reads a voter's agreement from), as if they knew it exactly. For a ward, county, state or federal seat it is still the town's electorate, so a statewide candidate is scored against one town.
why: The research rule scores a question by the support the candidate believes it has (Druckman, Jacobs and Ostermeier 2004 used Nixon's private polls), and no engine keeps a candidate's belief about how the town stands on a question.
replacement: The candidate's belief about support, read from the people they know and the polls and news they have received, so it leans toward their own side and their circle (Pereira, APSR 2021: local officials misjudge majority opinion and overestimate support for the policies they endorse) and toward the conservative position, more for Republicans (Broockman and Skovron 2018: Republicans overestimate support for the conservative position on every issue by over ten points and often by over twenty, Democrats by less), with the seat's own electorate (its ward, county or state) in place of the town's.

whatItFakes: platformSupportSlope is the study's domestic coefficient carried over, and the played total it is checked against does not reach the research's band. The research's C1 (docs/research/platform-emphasis-2026-10-30.md, as its quote verification restates it: +16% to +86% emphasis per 10 points of support), measured from what candidates said by record (messages and speeches on each question they hold a view on, silences included, each candidate offset by how many questions they hold a view on) over 42 candidates in four drawn places' years (run seed b6c9d59eda6a31f1, src/core2/campaign-platform-played.test.ts), gives -3% at the slope's value 0.035; with each campaign's lead chosen again from the recorded scores, -16% at 0 (the old rule), -10% at 0.015 and -3% at 0.028, 0.043 and 0.062. No slope in the research's spread brings it in. Every act carries the campaign's lead alone (SG-GOV-platform-emphasis-lead-only), so each candidate's emphasis is all on their top score, the fit within one candidate's questions has no finite value, and the pooled total is set by the differences between candidates; over every slope from 0.028 up the top score does not change. Earlier measures on score shares (-13% pooled, +345% to +712% within candidates) overshoot or miss for the same reasons: picking the top 3 with silences sharpens the slope, as the research's C1 warns.
why: The study followed one candidate who spoke on many issues in graded amounts; the played world's candidates each speak on one question, and their support varies mostly between candidates (a candidate on the town's minority side has low support on most questions), not between one candidate's questions. Which total C1 holds in a world of many candidates, and whether a campaign's acts should share its emphasis over the platform by score as the research's emphasis share has it, is the governing lead's ruling.
replacement: The slope measured into the C1 band once a campaign's acts share its emphasis over the platform by score (SG-GOV-platform-emphasis-lead-only's replacement), by the pooled total with each candidate's offset, and the played-year test holds the band again: pool item campaign-platform-emphasis-c1. Until then the test prints C1 and does not hold it (governing lead, Nov 2, under the CTO's Nov 1 ruling that an unmet calibration line is reported in the PR and carried to its own item, never tuned or widened to pass).

whatItFakes: A voter's stance on spending more on a budget line ("budget-line:<line>") is their lean times the line's party direction (budget-line-axes.json, GSS 2024 by party) and nothing else: no faith, degree or age term as the policy questions have, and no term for the town's overall wish to spend more or less on it. Every line therefore splits the electorate the same way, the share on the right of the town's lean order against the share on the left, so a candidate's support on every spending line they hold a view on is the same number, and the platform rule chooses among spending lines by conviction alone.
why: The opening-stance loadings (opening-stance-loadings.json, CES 2020) cover the survey's policy items only; no loading table exists for the GSS spending items, and the spending preferences in data/research/money are kept by party only.
replacement: Faith, degree and age loadings for each budget line from the GSS spending items (NATEDUC, NATHEAL, NATCRIME and the rest, 2024 cumulative file) and the national share wanting more spent on each, read into the opening stance by the views engine for named and counted voters alike.

whatItFakes: A candidate's platform score leaves out the research rule's record factor, (1 + platformRecordWeight x record(q)): a question the candidate's own votes, job or past acts bear on favorably scores no higher than one they have no record on.
why: The research (docs/research/platform-emphasis-2026-10-30.md, section 1 and the verified P4) multiplies the score by the record term with platformRecordWeight 0.5, TUNABLE, spread 0 to 1, from Sellers (APSR 1998), which gives only the direction; the first version scores conviction and support only.
replacement: record(q), 0 to 1, read from the candidate's recorded votes on the question (StanceReader.votesOn, the votes a voter's record reader already reads) and their job's tie to it, weighted by a platformRecordWeight row (TUNABLE, 0.5, spread 0 to 1, Sellers 1998), with C1 kept in its band with it on.

whatItFakes: Every campaign act that carries one question (a donor meeting, an event, an ad, a mailer, an evening of doors) carries the campaign's lead (platformLead), so everything a candidate chooses to say in a race is on one question, the top score of their platform; the other platform questions are heard only where the whole platform is (a door, an interview answer).
why: The research's emphasis share gives each platform question its score's share of the space in speeches, flyers, ads and news quotes (docs/research/platform-emphasis-2026-10-30.md, section 1), and no campaign engine yet takes its acts' topics in turn over the platform.
replacement: Each act's topic taken in turn over the platform, the question furthest behind its score's share of what the campaign has said so far (no roll), so a candidate's messages and speeches follow the score shares; C1 then measured from those records.

whatItFakes: Where the candidates' party sides differ (a general election between parties), a counted voter record's unpledged people still vote whole for its first place, as one person would; only where their sides are equal (no labels, or one party's primary) do they divide by each candidate's logistic share of their appeal (countedShareRule).
why: CTO ruling Nov 1, 22:10: each place's counted people are placed along the lean order where, voting first place, they split as the place voted in 2024 (orderPlacement), so a share on top counts that spread twice: in a draw of all 51, D.C. counted 0.193 Republican against 0.072, and a town at 0.20 counted 0.297.
replacement: A spread of leans within each counted record on the lean order (the residents it stands for over its own stretch of the order), so that races with and without party labels divide by one rule and the lean order's placement reads the same division.

whatItFakes: The federal share of Medicaid's part of a town member's care is paid to the medical seller by the federal treasury at the match in force (payMedicaidCare), counted against the federal health line, and the whole care, the federal leg included, against the state's welfare and Medicaid line; so each dollar is inside a budget line and no close pays it again. But the federal aid to the state stays a twelfth of the state's Census federal aid, which already holds the federal share of the state's Medicaid, so the state keeps that share of the town's care as well (the outside payees of the federal health line are paid that much less).
why: The aid flows pay each lower treasury a fixed twelfth of its Census revenue line (budgets-treasury.ts, treasury-spending.json aid); no aid flow reads a law, so the match cannot yet set the Medicaid portion of the aid.
replacement: The state treasury pays the seller the whole Medicaid part against its welfare and Medicaid line, and the federal share reaches the state as federal aid at the match in force: the Medicaid portion of the federal aid to the state is the match times the state's Medicaid care, read when the aid pays.

whatItFakes: A race's story names its seat's district only where the seat record numbers it ("State Senate District 4", a county board's District 3). A district the record names by place (Massachusetts' "1st Barnstable District", New Hampshire's "Belknap 01", Vermont's "Addison-1"), D.C.'s wards and a council's wards print the office only, as every race did before.
why: Words gave the numbered and at-large lines (Nov 1, 23:06 and 23:11); the bank has no piece that says a district by its own name or a ward, and the pool item elections-past-race-names-the-district asks only for those two.
replacement: A news and a headline piece for a district named by place and one for a ward, worded by Words, reading the seat's districtName and its office's seatTerm, so every district seat's story names its seat.

whatItFakes: A local race's petition asks at most petitionMaxShareOfVoters (10%) of the town's voters, at least one, wherever the law's count or the estimated median would ask more: one share for every place, not each place's own percentage, minimum and maximum.
why: The places' rows give a fixed count or a median estimate that does not scale with the town, so a town of a few dozen adults was asked for 30 signatures (Johnson, Minnesota). The rows' own formulas scale with the place's voters (Vermont 30 or 1% whichever is less; Iowa 2% minimum 10; North Dakota 10% maximum 300; North Carolina 10% maximum 200; Arizona 5% to 10%).
replacement: Each place's own petition formula read into data (its percentage, base, minimum and maximum) and applied to the town's voters, so the cap is the law's own and no common share is needed.

whatItFakes: The district of a town council or county board elected by district that the player's home is in is drawn from the home's household id over the body's district seats (homeDistrict), the same district every day, because no district map is read for local bodies; the player is offered only that district's seat. Every resident still votes in every district's race (the seats all cover the town).
why: Owner, Nov 1 playtest ("I should only be able to run for one council seat") under the CTO's town council seats ruling: by district, the player files only for their own district's seat. The repository holds a council's district seat count (council-election-method.ts) but no district boundaries, so which district a home is in cannot be read.
replacement: Read each local body's district boundaries (or its residents' precinct-to-district assignments) into data, place every home in its district, and have each district race's electorate be that district's residents; the player is offered the seat of the district their home is in.

whatItFakes: A local body's at-large seats up on one day are separate contests, one winner a seat; the player is offered the at-large race once, as the first of those seats' contests whose filing is open, and files for that seat, not for the race as a whole with the top vote-getters seated.
why: Owner, Nov 1 playtest: one council race, not one per seat. The elections engine holds a contest per seat; a pooled at-large race (each voter votes for up to the number of seats, the top finishers win) is a new count and ballot.
replacement: An at-large race as one contest for the body's seats up that day, where each voter may vote for as many candidates as there are seats and the top finishers are seated (the place's own rule), so every candidate, the player included, files once for the race.

whatItFakes: A bill's later chamber votes on the same floor day as its first, and only if the first passes (countVote takes each chamber in turn), so the evening before, nobody knows whether the later chamber will vote at all. Its members are not asked for their vote then; a sponsor asks only in the bill's first chamber, whose committee has met.
why: Asks whose bill never reaches a roll call are pulls no vote reads (pool item legislature-ask-skips-bills-the-committee-will-hold); the model gives a bill one floor day for every chamber.
replacement: A later chamber takes up a bill on a floor day of its own after the first chamber passes it, with its own committee meeting the evening before and its own asks.

whatItFakes: A governor the player plays never declares a state of emergency: the engine does not declare for them, and no office screen offers the declaration when a disaster is recorded in their state.
why: The engine never answers for the player (the desk rule); the office screen's offer is the play-first lane's (agreement 1-4).
replacement: An office-screen stop the day a federally declared disaster is recorded in the player governor's state, offering declareEmergency with the hazard record and the state's power named, or leaving it to the character.
